works.title: Mona Lisa
works.hook: Probably Lisa Gherardini, a Florentine merchant's wife. Leonardo kept working on it for years and never handed it over.

works.title: The Last Supper
works.hook: Painted on a dry wall, not wet plaster, so it began flaking within decades.

works.title: The Birth of Venus
works.hook: One of the first large paintings of a pagan myth since antiquity, rather than a religious scene.

works.title: Primavera
works.hook: Botanists have identified around 500 plants in it.

works.title: The Creation of Adam
works.hook: Part of the Sistine Chapel ceiling, painted 1508–12. The almost-touching fingers are among the most copied images in art.

works.title: The School of Athens
works.hook: Plato and Aristotle stand at the centre. Plato is often said to have Leonardo's face.

works.title: Venus of Urbino
works.hook: Venetian painting was about colour; Florence prized drawing. Titian is Venice's star.

works.title: The Ambassadors
works.hook: The smear across the floor is a stretched skull. Look at it from the side and it snaps into shape.

works.title: The Hunters in the Snow
works.hook: One of a series on the seasons of the year. Peasant life, painted with real affection.

works.title: The Garden of Earthly Delights
works.hook: Paradise on the left, a strange garden of pleasure in the middle, hell on the right.

works.title: The Arnolfini Portrait
works.hook: The mirror reflects two more figures in the doorway. Above it he wrote 'Jan van Eyck was here 1434'.
works.note: Instead of Italian classical ideals, van Eyck builds realism from thin oil glazes, picking out every fur lining, straw hat and stained-glass pane.
works.why: Fur linings, a convex mirror and a gleaming chandelier, all in thin oil glazes: the minute detail of Netherlandish painting.

works.title: Portrait of a Man (Self Portrait?)
works.hook: The original frame reads 'Als ich can', his motto. Many think it's van Eyck himself.
works.note: Painted in Bruges, it records every bristle of stubble and each bloodshot eye in fine oil, under a vermilion headdress that is really a chaperon, not a turban.
works.why: Every bristle of stubble and bloodshot vein rendered in glowing oil: the minute detail Early Netherlandish painters prized.

works.title: Léal Souvenir
works.hook: The carved stone parapet is painted so well it looks chipped and real.
works.note: Painted in oil on a single oak board, the sitter is set against flat black and studied with Netherlandish precision, down to the unreadable lines on his scroll.
works.why: Moist eyes, creased skin and inscriptions seemingly chiselled into a stone ledge: the minute detail oil painting made possible.

works.title: The Ghent Altarpiece
works.hook: Begun with his brother Hubert. It's one of the most stolen artworks in history.
works.note: Its meadows are painted plant by plant with almost scientific accuracy in glowing oil, a northern obsession with detail rather than Italian classical proportion.
works.why: Meadow flowers painted plant by plant and jewelled robes glowing in oil: Netherlandish devotion to minute, luminous detail.

works.title: The Madonna of Chancellor Rolin
works.note: Beyond the loggia, a minutely detailed river city, probably Rolin's hometown of Autun, unfolds with palaces, a towered bridge and hazy distant mountains.
works.why: A miniature river city with bridge, towers and tiny figures beyond the loggia: Early Netherlandish oil detail at its finest.

works.title: The Night Watch
works.hook: Actually a daytime scene. Darkened varnish gave it the nickname.
works.note: A group portrait commissioned by Captain Banninck Cocq's militia for their Amsterdam hall, made dramatic by pools of light and shadow and a company marching out.
works.why: Officers stride out of deep shadow into bright light as the company moves off: Baroque drama of motion and contrast.

works.title: Self-Portrait with Two Circles
works.hook: Free to see at Kenwood on Hampstead Heath. Nobody agrees what the circles mean.
works.note: Rembrandt grips palette, brushes and maulstick in a fur-lined robe, even scratching lines into the wet oil paint: a Dutch master asserting his own genius.
works.why: A strongly lit face above a dark robe, in thick, rough paint: the Baroque play of light against shadow.

works.title: Girl with a Pearl Earring
works.hook: Not a portrait but a 'tronie': a study of a character or expression.
works.note: Vermeer modelled her face and exotic turban in oil paint with natural ultramarine, letting her glow out of a dark background of green glaze over black.
works.why: Her face glows out of a dark, plain background: the Baroque love of light emerging from shadow.

works.title: The Milkmaid
works.hook: Quiet everyday life, lit from a window on the left: pure Vermeer.
works.note: Tiny dots of paint make the bread crust glitter, and Vermeer chose costly ultramarine ground from lapis lazuli for the blues, all in oil on canvas.
works.why: Strong window light models the maid's solid figure, half her face in shadow: Baroque realism of everyday life.

works.title: View of Delft
works.note: Vermeer painted his hometown from across the water, boats moored with sails lowered as sunlight bathes the Nieuwe Kerk tower: a proud Dutch trading city.
works.why: Shadowed buildings along the water, sunlit roofs and tower beyond: Baroque contrast of light and shade under a dramatic sky.

works.title: Las Meninas
works.hook: The king and queen appear only in the mirror at the back. Velázquez paints himself at the easel.
works.note: A huge oil canvas from the Spanish court: the five-year-old Infanta Margaret Theresa surrounded by maids of honour, a chaperone, a bodyguard, two dwarfs and a dog.
works.why: Light falls from a side window across the Infanta while the room behind sinks into shadow: Baroque theatre of light.

works.title: The Rokeby Venus
works.hook: A suffragette slashed it with a meat cleaver in 1914. It was repaired.
works.note: Cupid holds the mirror in which Venus's face is only a blur, a rare painted nude from Spain, where the Inquisition frowned on them.
works.why: Venus's pale, curving back glows against dark grey sheets: a sensuous Baroque play of light against shadow.

works.title: The Calling of Saint Matthew
works.hook: A beam of light follows Christ's pointing hand into a gloomy tax office.
works.note: For his first major church commission, Caravaggio turned a Gospel story into a sudden, real-life moment of conversion, staged in stark contrasts of light and dark.
works.why: A single shaft of light cuts across a dim room towards Matthew: Baroque drama through stark light and dark.

works.title: Supper at Emmaus
works.hook: The fruit basket teeters off the table edge, right into your space.

works.title: Judith Slaying Holofernes
works.hook: Artemisia was one of the most successful painters of her day, and the first woman admitted to Florence's Academy of Drawing.
works.note: Following Caravaggio, she floods the struggle with harsh light against deep darkness, making Judith a physically active killer rather than a demure heroine.
works.why: Blood spurts as a brutal struggle is lit harshly against pitch darkness: Baroque drama at its most violent.

works.title: The Elevation of the Cross
works.hook: All muscle and diagonal strain: Baroque drama at full volume.
works.note: A huge oil-on-panel triptych for a church high altar in Antwerp, painted just after Rubens's years in Italy in the spirit of the Counter-Reformation.
works.why: Muscular men strain to haul the cross up a steep diagonal: Baroque drama built from movement and physical effort.

works.title: The Swing
works.hook: A flying shoe, a hidden admirer in the bushes: a flirtatious private commission.
works.note: A courtier ordered this picture of his mistress, and Fragonard filled it with billowing skirts, garden bushes and a stone cupid raising a finger to its lips.
works.why: Frothy pink silk, a flying slipper and lush garden foliage: Rococo's playful, pastel world of love and leisure.

works.title: Pilgrimage to Cythera
works.hook: The French Academy invented a new category for it: the fête galante.
works.note: Elegant couples drift towards a golden boat while cupids flutter around them, all in light, wispy brushwork: aristocratic pleasure after Louis XIV's sombre final years.
works.why: Elegant couples and fluttering cupids in soft, feathery brushwork: the Rococo world of love and leisure.

works.title: The Toilet of Venus
works.place: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
works.hook: Painted for Madame de Pompadour, Louis XV's favourite and Boucher's great patron.
works.note: Made for the bathroom of Château de Bellevue, it shows putti fussing with Venus's hair and pearls beside a pair of doves, all in soft pastel colours.
works.why: Putti, pearls, doves and pink velvet in soft pastel tones: the playful, luxurious prettiness at the heart of Rococo.

works.title: Marriage A-la-Mode: 1, The Marriage Settlement
works.hook: Scene one of six: a money-for-title marriage that ends in disaster.
works.note: Made to be engraved as prints, it mocks English snobbery: a gouty, bankrupt earl points proudly at a family tree reaching back to William the Conqueror.
works.why: A gouty earl points to his family tree while a merchant studies the contract: Georgian satire of marrying for money.

works.title: Mr and Mrs Andrews
works.hook: Look at Mrs Andrews' lap: it was left unfinished.
works.note: Gainsborough sets a newly married Suffolk couple beside the actual fields of their estate, probably part of Mrs Andrews' dowry, fusing portrait and English landscape.
works.why: A fashionably dressed couple posed proudly beside their own cornfields: Georgian gentry portraiture celebrating land and status.

works.title: The Blue Boy
works.hook: Sold to an American collector in 1921. Huge crowds came to say goodbye.
works.why: Gainsborough dressed the boy in 17th-century clothes as a tribute to the Baroque painter Van Dyck, but he painted it in 1770.

works.title: Whistlejacket
works.hook: Life-size, on a blank background. Stubbs knew horse anatomy from dissection.
works.note: Commissioned by the Marquess of Rockingham, this prized English racehorse rears up in oils with no rider, no landscape and no decorative frills.
works.why: A life-size prize racehorse rearing against a plain background: the gentry's pride in its bloodstock, painted as portrait.

works.title: An Experiment on a Bird in the Air Pump
works.hook: Science as drama, lit by a single candle. Will the bird survive?
works.note: Wright treats a natural philosopher's experiment with the reverence once reserved for religious and historical scenes, capturing Britain's Enlightenment and Industrial Revolution.
works.why: Well-dressed onlookers gather by candlelight round a scientific demonstration: Georgian polite society absorbed in Enlightenment science.

works.title: The Hay Wain
works.hook: It failed to sell in London, then won a gold medal at the Paris Salon of 1824.
works.note: Constable painted the real countryside beside his father's Flatford Mill on the River Stour, working up the six-foot canvas from a full-size oil sketch.
works.why: Billowing clouds and flecks of white light over a Suffolk river: the Romantic devotion to nature, deeply felt.

works.title: The Fighting Temeraire
works.hook: A Trafalgar warship towed to the breakers by a steam tug. Voted Britain's favourite painting in 2005.
works.note: Turner sets the pale, ghostly warship against a blazing sunset whose red is echoed in the river and the tug's smoke: the end of an era as emotion.
works.why: A ghostly old warship towed by a blackened steam tug under a blazing sunset: history turned into Romantic feeling.

works.title: Rain, Steam and Speed
works.hook: Look closely: a tiny hare runs ahead of the train.
works.note: A steam train, probably a Great Western Firefly-class engine, charges across Maidenhead bridge into rain and mist: Turner made the industrial age sublime.
works.why: A dark locomotive bursts through blurred rain and golden haze: the overwhelming, sublime atmosphere Romantic painters sought.

works.title: The Slave Ship
works.note: A blood-red sunset and looming typhoon engulf a slave ship as shackled victims sink amid fish and gulls, recalling the 1781 Zong massacre.
works.why: A blood-red sky and churning storm swallow the ship: nature's terrifying power, the Romantic sublime.

works.title: Wanderer above the Sea of Fog
works.hook: Seen from behind, the figure invites you to stand in his place.
works.note: The rocky peaks come from the Elbe Sandstone Mountains, sketched outdoors then rearranged in the studio into a sublime, imagined panorama of mist.
works.why: A lone figure seen from behind faces an endless sea of fog: nature as vast, mysterious and sublime.

works.title: Liberty Leading the People
works.hook: Painted to mark the July Revolution of 1830. Restored in 2024.
works.note: Freely brushed colour, an allegorical bare-breasted Liberty and fallen bodies on a barricade turn a real Paris uprising into passionate, heroic drama.
works.why: Liberty strides over a barricade of fallen bodies, flag raised: Romantic passion and heroism at full emotional pitch.

works.title: The Raft of the Medusa
works.hook: Based on a real 1816 shipwreck scandal. Géricault interviewed survivors.
works.note: Géricault studied dying and dead flesh in hospitals and morgues, then filled a vast over-life-size canvas with despair that broke with calm Neoclassical order.
works.why: Desperate bodies heaped on a wave-tossed raft, reaching towards a distant ship: Romantic drama of extreme emotion.

works.title: The Third of May 1808
works.hook: Faceless soldiers, a man with arms flung out like a crucifixion: a model for every anti-war picture after.
works.note: Commissioned by Spain's provisional government, a square lantern blazes on a labourer in a plain white shirt facing a French firing squad.
works.why: A lantern blazes on a man flinging up his arms before a faceless firing squad: raw emotion over calm order.

works.title: The Nightmare
works.hook: Shown at the Royal Academy in 1782, it caused a sensation.
works.note: An ape-like demon crouches on a sleeping woman's chest as a half-hidden horse looks on: Fuseli painted irrational dread, not polite Georgian society.
works.why: A demon squats on a sleeping woman as a wild-eyed horse peers in: Romantic fascination with dread and the irrational.

works.title: The Gleaners
works.hook: Poor women picking up leftover grain, painted with the dignity usually given to heroes. Some critics found it political.
works.note: Three real peasant women from around Barbizon stoop in the foreground while the rich harvest glows in the sunlit distance: rural poverty, not medieval legend.
works.why: Three peasant women stooping over stubble, their heavy labour shown plainly: rural poverty as the Realist subject.

works.title: The Stone Breakers
works.hook: Lost in the Second World War, probably in the 1945 bombing of Dresden. Courbet reportedly said he could not paint an angel, having never seen one.
works.note: Courbet saw these two road labourers near Maisières and painted them unidealised, faces turned away, in patched and tattered clothes.
works.why: Ordinary labourers in tattered clothes, shown unidealised: exactly what Realism set out to paint.

works.title: Olympia
works.hook: A modern Paris courtesan in the pose of Titian's Venus. The 1865 Salon was outraged.
works.note: Broad, quick brushstrokes and harsh studio light flatten a real model, Victorine Meurent, who stares straight back at us: no idealised goddess, just modern Paris.
works.why: A nude courtesan in flat, harsh light stares boldly back at us: a modern woman, painted without idealising.

works.title: Le Déjeuner sur l'herbe
works.hook: Rejected by the Salon, shown at the 1863 Salon des Refusés.
works.note: A nude woman lunches with two fully dressed modern men, painted with visible, unhidden brushstrokes, nothing like the smooth, flawless nudes of Cabanel or Ingres.
works.why: Two men in modern clothes beside a frankly unidealised nude: Realism dragging an old-master theme into the present day.

works.title: Impression, Sunrise
works.hook: The painting that gave the movement its name, the harbour of Le Havre.
works.note: Painted from his window, loose strokes only suggest the scene: those misty shapes are steamship smokestacks and cranes melting into the haze.
works.why: Loose, quick strokes blur harbour, boats and sun into hazy morning light: catching one fleeting moment rather than every detail.

works.title: Woman with a Parasol
works.hook: Monet's wife Camille and son Jean, caught in a breezy moment.
works.note: Painted outdoors in a few hours, its quick, splashy brushstrokes catch the wind tugging at Camille's veil and dress, a fleeting moment rather than a finished story.
works.why: Quick, broken brushstrokes catch wind and sunlight on a breezy hillside: the fleeting outdoor moment Impressionism chased.

works.title: Water Lilies
works.place: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
works.hook: Monet painted his Giverny pond around 250 times.
works.note: Monet was still recording what he saw: light and reflections on the lily pond in his own Giverny garden, even as cataracts clouded his eyes.
works.why: Loose, visible strokes catch shimmering reflections on the pond's surface: Impressionism's pursuit of fleeting light.

works.title: Bal du moulin de la Galette
works.hook: A Sunday dance in Montmartre, with dappled sunlight through the trees.
works.note: Renoir painted it on the spot, with friends and fellow painters posing among the dancers, in quick, fluid strokes of flickering light.
works.why: Flickering, sun-dappled light on Sunday dancers in loose, fluid strokes: Impressionism's mix of passing light and modern Parisian leisure.

works.title: Luncheon of the Boating Party
works.hook: The woman with the dog is Aline Charigot, later Renoir's wife.
works.note: Renoir's friends lounge on a restaurant balcony by the Seine at Chatou, painted with fluid brushwork and flickering light: a modern day out, not a legend.
works.why: Dappled sunlight flickers over friends lunching by the river, in loose, feathery strokes: Impressionist modern leisure caught in light.

works.title: Paris Street; Rainy Day
works.hook: Haussmann's brand-new Paris boulevards. Caillebotte also funded his friends' exhibitions.
works.note: Shown at the Third Impressionist Exhibition, it makes modern city life the subject: 24 mostly bourgeois pedestrians, led by a couple sharing an umbrella.
works.why: Fashionable Parisians stroll a newly built boulevard under umbrellas: modern city life as the Impressionist subject.

works.title: The Cradle
works.hook: Shown at the first Impressionist exhibition in 1874. Morisot showed in all but one of the eight.
works.note: Morisot painted her sister Edma watching over baby Blanche using few colours and a fluid brushstroke, a private, everyday moment rather than a story.
works.why: A mother watching her sleeping baby, in few colours and fluid strokes: the Impressionist eye for private, everyday modern life.

works.title: The Child's Bath
works.hook: The high viewpoint and bold patterns come from Japanese prints.
works.note: Cassatt makes a modern everyday routine the whole subject, a mother bathing her child, at a time when French health campaigns urged regular bathing after cholera outbreaks.
works.why: A mother washing her child's feet, seen from above: an intimate everyday moment, the stuff of Impressionist modern life.

works.title: A Bar at the Folies-Bergère
works.hook: The reflection in the mirror doesn't quite add up. That's the puzzle.
works.note: A real barmaid, Suzon, stands before a mirror reflecting the music-hall crowd, with a trapeze artist's green feet dangling in the top corner: pure modern Paris.
works.why: A mirror behind the barmaid reflects a glittering music-hall crowd in loose strokes: modern Parisian pleasure, Impressionist style.

works.title: The Starry Night
works.place: Museum of Modern Art, New York
works.hook: The view from his window at the asylum in Saint-Rémy. The village was largely invented.
works.note: A swirling sky and a flame-like cypress, exaggerated in scale, turn a night view into feeling; the brightest 'star' beside the tree is actually Venus.
works.why: A swirling sky and an exaggerated, flame-like cypress: one painter's personal vision pushing far beyond the view he saw.

works.title: Sunflowers
works.hook: Painted in Arles to decorate Gauguin's room. There are several versions.
works.note: Fifteen sunflowers, from bud to wilting seed head, are built up in thick impasto and almost nothing but yellows, signed 'Vincent' in blue on the vase.
works.why: Thick, ridged impasto in almost nothing but yellows: colour pushed for expression, a Post-Impressionist hallmark.

works.title: The Potato Eaters
works.hook: His dark early Dutch period, before Paris turned his palette bright.

works.title: Café Terrace at Night
works.hook: A night scene with no black paint: blues, violets and yellows.
works.note: Van Gogh set up his easel on the Place du Forum in Arles in September 1888, pitting a glowing yellow terrace against a star-studded blue sky.
works.why: A glowing yellow terrace against a deep blue starry sky: Post-Impressionist colour chosen for feeling, not description.

works.title: The Card Players
works.hook: One of five versions. Solid, still, built from blocks of colour.
works.note: Cézanne's models were local farmhands, some working on his family's Jas de Bouffan estate, shown as still and weighty as the table between them.
works.why: Two still, solid players pared down to essentials around a single bottle: forms simplified into lasting, weighty structure.

works.title: Mont Sainte-Victoire
works.hook: Cézanne painted this Provence mountain dozens of times.
works.note: Cézanne builds the mountain from geometry and blocks of colour, seeking its solid, lasting structure rather than the passing light effects the Impressionists chased.
works.why: The mountain and fields built from blocks and patches of colour: simplified, solid forms on Cézanne's own Post-Impressionist path.

works.title: A Sunday on La Grande Jatte
works.hook: Two years of work in tiny dots of colour: pointillism.
works.note: Seurat applied the colour theories of scientists like Chevreul and Rood, planning his Parisians through numerous drawings and oil sketches rather than catching a passing moment.
works.why: Thousands of tiny dots of colour build stiff, carefully planned figures: Seurat's scientific Post-Impressionist method.

works.title: Bathers at Asnières
works.hook: Factory chimneys in the distance: workers relaxing by the Seine.
works.note: No quick outdoor sketch: Seurat built this canvas, three metres wide, in his studio from over a dozen oil studies, and the Salon still rejected it.
works.why: Still, statuesque bathers in profile, set in a formal, ordered layout: fleeting modern leisure rebuilt as calm, lasting design.

works.title: Where Do We Come From? What Are We? Where Are We Going?
works.hook: Painted in Tahiti and read right to left, from birth to old age.
works.note: Vivid flat colour on coarse sackcloth carries questions from Gauguin's schoolboy catechism class: a symbolic allegory of life, not an observed scene.
works.why: Flat zones of vivid colour and symbolic figures across one long frieze: bold, simplified forms carrying ideas, not observation.

works.title: At the Moulin Rouge
works.hook: Lautrec painted himself into the background: the short man in the bowler hat.
works.note: May Milton's face glows an eerie green at the right edge and Jane Avril's hair flames red-orange: colour pushed for effect, not faithful to nature.
works.why: A woman's face lit an eerie acid green at the right edge: colour pushed for effect, a Post-Impressionist hallmark.

works.title: The Great Wave off Kanagawa
works.hook: A print, so many museums own one, including the British Museum. Find tiny Mount Fuji.
works.note: A woodblock print from Hokusai's Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji, its deep blue is Prussian blue, a pigment newly arrived in Japan.
works.why: Blocks of Prussian blue and a crest of claw-like foam: the bold, graphic language of the Japanese woodblock print.

works.title: Fine Wind, Clear Morning (Red Fuji)
works.hook: From the same series as the Great Wave: Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji.
works.note: A woodblock print, not an oil painting: flat blocks of Prussian blue and Bengal red catch Fuji turning red at sunrise on a clear early-autumn morning.
works.why: Flat blocks of Prussian blue and red, printed rather than painted: an Edo woodblock landscape print.

works.title: Plum Park in Kameido
works.hook: Van Gogh copied this print in oil in 1887.
works.note: A woodblock print from Hiroshige's One Hundred Famous Views of Edo: a giant plum branch, cropped by the frame, lets us peer through at blossom-viewers beyond.
works.why: A huge plum branch cropped by the frame, in flat colour with crisp outlines: hallmarks of an Edo woodblock print.

works.title: Sudden Shower over Shin-Ōhashi Bridge
works.hook: Rain as fine diagonal lines. Van Gogh copied this one too.
works.note: From Hiroshige's woodblock series One Hundred Famous Views of Edo: figures under hats, umbrellas and straw capes hurry across while a raftsman punts below.
works.why: Rain carved as fine parallel lines over areas of flat colour: woodblock printmaking at its most graphic.

works.title: Folding screen with cherry blossom (detail)
works.hook: Rinpa style: bold, decorative nature against gold leaf.
works.note: A folding screen to divide a room and set the mood for tea gatherings, it follows Ogata Kōrin's style, which Hōitsu revived in Edo.
works.why: Flat, stylised cherry blossom against broad gold leaf: the Rinpa screen style Hōitsu brought to Edo.

works.title: The Kiss
works.hook: Real gold leaf. The height of Klimt's 'golden period'.
works.note: After seeing Byzantine mosaics in Ravenna, Klimt flattened the lovers into shimmering pattern, the man's robe covered in geometric shapes, an icon of the Vienna Secession.
works.why: Lovers wrapped in shimmering gold leaf and flat ornamental pattern: the decorative splendour of Vienna 1900.

works.title: Portrait of Elisabeth Lederer
works.hook: Sold at Sotheby's New York in November 2025 for $236.4m, a record for modern art at auction.
works.note: Behind her floats an ornamental field of figures drawn from Chinese ceramics and Peking opera, echoing the East Asian art Klimt collected.
works.why: Flat ornament fills the background around the figure: the decorative signature of Vienna 1900.

works.title: Woman with a Hat
works.place: San Francisco Museum of Modern Art
works.hook: Shown at the 1905 Salon d'Automne, where the 'wild beasts' got their name.
works.note: Matisse gave his wife Amélie a face of unnatural colours, split by a green line, under an imaginative hat: colour freed from describing reality.
works.why: Green streaks and mauve blotches across her face: wild, unnatural colour for its own sake, the Fauve signature.

works.title: Dance
works.hook: Just three colours: red, green, blue. Commissioned by the Moscow collector Sergei Shchukin.
works.note: Five nude figures whirl hand in hand against a very simplified landscape, painted to hang on the staircase of a Moscow mansion and convey joyous release.
works.why: Five red nudes whirl against flat bands of blue and green: Fauvist colour, pure, bold and unnatural.

works.title: The Scream
works.hook: Munch made several versions. He described sensing 'an infinite scream passing through nature'.
works.note: Munch's diary recalls the clouds over the Oslofjord turning 'blood red'; he painted that feeling, not the view, in oil, tempera and pastel on cardboard.
works.why: An agonised, skull-like face under a blood-red sky: inner anxiety distorting the whole landscape around it.

works.title: Saturn Devouring His Son
works.hook: One of the 'Black Paintings' Goya painted straight onto the walls of his house.
works.note: Goya painted it for no patron and gave it no title or explanation: a private vision of horror drawn from the myth of Saturn eating his children.
works.why: A wild-eyed giant biting into a headless body, in dark, rough paint: Romantic horror and raw emotion.

works.title: Les Demoiselles d'Avignon
works.place: Museum of Modern Art, New York
works.hook: Even Picasso's friends were shocked. It opened the door to Cubism.
works.note: Five women from a Barcelona brothel are broken into flat, angular planes, their faces drawn from Iberian sculpture and African masks.
works.why: Bodies sliced into flat, angular planes, with faces like masks: the fractured forms that led to Cubism.

works.title: Nude Descending a Staircase, No. 2
works.hook: Mocked at New York's 1913 Armory Show as 'an explosion in a shingle factory'.
works.note: Inspired by Marey's motion photography, Duchamp stacked fractured, overlapping figures in browns and ochres to show a body moving step by step.
works.why: A body broken into overlapping ochre planes, repeated step by step: Cubist fragmentation set in motion.

works.title: Udnie
works.hook: Inspired by a dancer Picabia saw on a ship to New York.
works.note: Picabia breaks movement into colliding, curving planes with metallic, machine-like reflections, a fractured form shaped by Futurist dynamism and Duchamp's mechanical imagery.
works.why: Curving, interlocking planes of colour shatter a dancer's movement into fragments: Cubist faceting set in motion.

works.title: Contrast of Forms
works.hook: Léger's chunky cylinders earned the nickname 'Tubism'.
works.note: Tubes, cones and cubes in bold blocks of primary colour, plus green, black and white, make Léger's Cubism loud where Picasso and Braque's early Cubism was muted.
works.why: Cones, cubes and cylinders in bright colour with stark black and white: Léger's bold, contrasting take on Cubism.

works.title: Composition VII
works.hook: Kandinsky named his biggest works 'Compositions', like a composer.
works.note: Painted in about four days on a canvas three metres wide, it distils themes like the Flood and Judgement Day into pure colour and line.
works.why: A storm of colours, lines and shapes, its biblical themes barely legible: painting moving beyond recognisable depiction.

works.title: Black Square
works.hook: At its first showing it hung high across a corner, where a Russian home places an icon.
works.note: Malevich called it the 'zero point of painting': no object at all, only form, in his bid to free art from 'the ballast of the objective world'.
works.why: A single black square on white, depicting nothing at all: pure shape with no recognisable subject.

works.title: Suprematist Composition: White on White
works.place: Museum of Modern Art, New York
works.note: A tilted white square floats on a slightly warmer white ground, with no colour, depth or volume; Malevich meant white to suggest infinity.
works.why: Just a tilted white square on a white ground, no subject at all: abstraction reduced to pure shape.

works.title: Broadway Boogie Woogie
works.place: Museum of Modern Art, New York
works.hook: New York's grid of streets and jazz rhythms, after he moved there in 1940.
works.note: Instead of dream imagery or dripped paint, Mondrian divided the canvas into a precise grid of small squares, his tribute to the boogie-woogie he loved.
works.why: A grid of lines broken into many small coloured squares, with no recognisable subject: pure colour, line and rhythm.

works.title: Composition II in Red, Blue and Yellow
works.hook: Only black lines, white, and the three primary colours.
works.note: Mondrian balances asymmetric flat planes against thick black bars as a harmony of opposites, with no objects, dreams or hidden figures to decode.
works.why: A big red square, small blue and yellow blocks and black lines: pure colour and shape, depicting nothing.

works.title: Composition
works.hook: Mondrian in Paris, breaking trees and buildings into a grid on the way to pure abstraction.
works.note: Mondrian absorbed Picasso and Braque's Cubism after arriving in Paris in 1912, but saw it only as a 'port of call' on his journey towards pure abstraction.

works.title: L.H.O.O.Q.
works.hook: A cheap Mona Lisa postcard with a moustache added. The letters make a rude pun in French.
works.note: No painting skill on show: Duchamp simply pencilled onto a found reproduction, a 'rectified readymade' mocking reverence for great art.
works.why: A cheap Mona Lisa postcard with a pencilled moustache and beard: Dada's mocking jab at reverence for great art.

works.title: Interchange
works.hook: Reportedly sold privately in 2015 for about $300m.
works.note: De Kooning's quick, gestural marks, learned from Franz Kline, almost swallow a fleshy pink seated woman as his work shifts towards abstract urban landscapes.
works.why: Slashing, energetic brushstrokes collide across a large canvas: the gestural energy of 1950s New York painting.

works.title: Campbell's Soup Cans
works.place: Museum of Modern Art, New York
works.hook: 32 canvases, one for each flavour then on sale.
works.note: Hand-painted supermarket packaging, first shown in Los Angeles in 1962 on narrow ledges like grocery items on a shelf.
works.why: Thirty-two near-identical soup cans, copied from supermarket packaging: everyday consumer imagery turned into Pop Art.

works.title: Salvator Mundi
works.hook: $450.3m at Christie's in 2017, still the auction record. Some experts doubt it's by Leonardo.
works.note: Bought for just $1,175 at a New Orleans auction in 2005 as a damaged later copy, it was heavily restored before its record-breaking sale.

works.title: The Shipwreck
works.hook: Tiny people against overwhelming nature: the Romantic 'sublime'.
works.note: Probably inspired by the Earl of Abergavenny's sinking off Weymouth that year, Turner turned current news into drama and showed it in his own London gallery.
works.why: Mountainous waves toss small boats beside a sinking ship: Romantic awe at nature's terrifying, sublime power.

works.title: Ophelia
works.hook: Elizabeth Siddal posed for hours in a bath of water and caught a severe cold. The plants were painted outdoors by the Hogsmill River in Surrey.
works.note: Millais painted the riverbank for up to 11 hours a day over five months, choosing each floating flower to match Shakespeare's description of Ophelia's garland.
works.why: Every leaf, petal and reed painted in jewel-bright, minute detail around a Shakespearean heroine: the Pre-Raphaelite formula.

works.title: The Lady of Shalott
works.hook: From Tennyson's poem. Waterhouse painted it decades after the Brotherhood, keeping its love of literature and detail.
works.note: Every detail tells Tennyson's story: she sits on the tapestry she wove, beside a crucifix and three candles, two already blown out.
works.why: Tennyson's heroine on her woven tapestry, with crucifix and snuffed candles: the Pre-Raphaelite love of literary subjects.

works.title: Proserpine
works.hook: The model is Jane Morris. The pomegranate means Proserpine must stay in the underworld.
works.note: Rossetti painted at least eight versions of this one myth between 1871 and 1882, a poetic legend lovingly reworked rather than modern Paris life.
works.why: A mythical queen in a blue gown holds a bitten pomegranate: Pre-Raphaelite rich colour and literary subject.

works.title: Beata Beatrix
works.hook: Rossetti's memorial to his wife, Elizabeth Siddal, painted after her death.
works.note: A red dove, messenger of love, brings a white poppy, symbol of the laudanum that killed Siddal, as Beatrice sits in a trance of 'spiritual transfiguration'.
works.why: A medieval heroine from Dante, with a symbolic dove and poppy: the Pre-Raphaelite love of literary subjects.

works.title: Norham Castle, Sunrise
works.hook: So loose it looks abstract. Turner never exhibited it.
works.note: One of Turner's unfinished colour reworkings of his own print series, the Liber Studiorum, showing the castle above the River Tweed melting into light.
works.why: The castle all but dissolves into soft washes of dawn light: nature felt as pure atmosphere and emotion.

works.title: Snow Storm - Steam-Boat off a Harbour’s Mouth
works.hook: Turner claimed he had himself tied to a ship's mast to experience the storm.
works.note: Black steam merges into a whirling vortex of snow and sea, painted so loosely that critics mocked it as 'soapsuds and whitewash'.
works.why: A tiny steamboat swallowed by a whirling vortex of snow and sea: the Romantic sublime of nature's overwhelming power.

works.title: Flatford Mill
works.hook: Painted near Constable's family mill in Suffolk: 'Constable Country'.
works.note: A working river observed closely: one boy unhitches the tow-rope from a barge while another sits astride the tow-horse, near Constable's Suffolk village.
works.why: A sunlit Suffolk river with towering trees and broad sky, closely observed: the Romantic attachment to native landscape.

works.title: Newton
works.medium: Colour print, ink and watercolour on paper
works.hook: Blake shows the scientist as a heroic but blinkered figure, measuring the world with dividers.
works.note: Not a painting but a colour print: Blake puts Newton naked on a rock at the bottom of the sea, a visionary attack on Enlightenment science.
works.why: A naked Newton crouches on a strange sea-floor rock, absorbed in his compasses: a visionary, imagined world, not observed fact.

works.title: The Great Day of His Wrath
works.hook: John Martin's apocalypse paintings drew crowds like blockbuster films.
works.note: Following Revelation, Martin shows mountains torn from their places and a whole city crashing into an abyss, part of his Last Judgement triptych.
works.why: Mountains torn up and a city tumbling into a fiery abyss: the Romantic sublime on an apocalyptic scale.

works.title: The Painter and his Pug
works.hook: Hogarth's self-portrait with his pug, Trump.
works.note: Look at the palette: it shows Hogarth's serpentine 'Line of Beauty', his own theory of art, set beside books the pug ignores.
works.why: A cheeky pug sits beside the painter's own oval portrait: the down-to-earth wit of Georgian Britain.

works.title: O the Roast Beef of Old England
works.note: Arrested as a spy while sketching in Calais, Hogarth took revenge: starving French soldiers and a fat friar gaze hungrily as English beef is carried past.
works.why: Ragged, hungry French soldiers and a fat friar ogle a side of English beef: patriotic Georgian satire.

works.title: Haymakers
works.hook: Stubbs is best known for horses; here he turns to farm workers at harvest.
works.note: Painted in oil on a wooden panel for his pastoral Haymakers and Reapers series, it shows the English hay harvest as a calm idyll, not Romantic drama.
works.why: Neatly dressed farm workers posed in a calm, orderly frieze: a polished, genteel Georgian view of rural life.

works.title: Giovanna Baccelli
works.note: Commissioned by the Duke of Dorset, the Italian dancer wears her ballet costume and stage make-up, caught in a dynamic pose with lightly flicked brushstrokes.
works.why: A dancer in stage costume, posed with lively animation in light, flicked strokes: elegant Georgian society portraiture.

works.title: Poplars on the Epte
works.hook: One of a series: Monet painted the same trees at different times of day.
works.note: Monet painted from a boat studio on the Epte, and even bought the trees when they were auctioned before he had finished painting them outdoors.
works.why: Tall poplars and their river reflections in quick, broken strokes: Monet chasing the light of a single moment.

works.title: Little Dancer Aged Fourteen
works.medium: Painted bronze with muslin and silk on wooden base
works.hook: The only sculpture Degas ever exhibited, first shown in wax in 1881. This bronze was cast after his death, with a real fabric tutu.
works.note: Her model was Marie van Goethem, a Paris Opera Ballet student, shown mid-exercise rather than angelic, and some viewers thought her a deliberate image of ugliness.
works.why: A young ballet student in a real fabric tutu and ribbon: Impressionism's eye for everyday modern Paris life.

works.title: The Gardener Vallier
works.hook: One of Cézanne's last paintings: the figure built from blocks of colour.
works.note: Cézanne's gardener at his Les Lauves studio, built from short patches of colour, with bare or thinly covered canvas left showing through.

works.title: Farms near Auvers
works.hook: Painted in Van Gogh's final weeks at Auvers-sur-Oise, 1890.
works.note: Hasty brushwork and a bare sky show van Gogh racing to capture mossy thatched roofs echoed by the hills behind, on a long double-square canvas.
works.why: Mossy thatched roofs echoed by the hills, in loose, rapid strokes: a personal, rhythmic way of seeing landscape.

works.title: Clarinet and Bottle of Rum on a Mantelpiece
works.hook: Analytic Cubism: objects split into facets in a narrow palette of browns and greys.
works.note: In 1911, when Braque's and Picasso's canvases became almost impossible to tell apart, Braque showed a clarinet on a mantelpiece from several viewpoints at once.

works.title: Dynamic Suprematism
works.hook: Malevich's Suprematism: pure geometric shapes, no objects at all.

works.title: Cossacks
works.hook: Riders and lances are still just visible. Kandinsky was on the edge of pure abstraction.
works.note: A cheerful rainbow, jagged mountains and birds float as black lines and blotches of primary colour, with no perspective: Kandinsky wanted painting to feel spiritual.
works.why: Black lines and blotches of primary colour barely hint at riders and a rainbow: a picture poised between scene and abstraction.

works.title: Composition with Yellow, Blue and Red
works.hook: Black lines and primary colours: the classic De Stijl look.
works.note: Nothing dreamlike or hidden here: Mondrian restricted himself to red, blue and yellow with straight black lines, an art of pure balance he called Neoplasticism.
works.why: Straight black lines and blocks of primary colour on white: pure balance, with nothing taken from nature.

works.title: Fountain
works.hook: A shop-bought urinal signed 'R. Mutt'. The original was lost; Tate's is a 1964 replica.
works.note: Duchamp chose a factory-made porcelain urinal, turned it on its back and called it art: the artist's choice alone made it a sculpture.
works.why: An ordinary factory urinal, turned on its back and signed 'R. Mutt': Dada's anti-art provocation in its purest form.

works.title: Metamorphosis of Narcissus
works.hook: Dalí showed this to Sigmund Freud in London in 1938.
works.note: Dalí doubles the crouching Narcissus with a stone hand holding a cracked egg that sprouts a narcissus flower, a visual trick from his 'paranoiac-critical' method.
works.why: A kneeling figure mirrored by a stone hand holding a cracked egg: a dreamlike double image from the unconscious.

works.title: Lobster Telephone
works.medium: Steel, plaster, rubber, resin and paper
works.hook: Made with the collector Edward James. A working phone with a sculpted lobster for a receiver.
works.note: Dalí fused two ordinary objects because lobsters and telephones both had strong sexual connotations for him, a classic Surrealist object rather than a pure abstract form.
works.why: A plaster lobster laid on a working telephone: two unrelated objects joined to stir the unconscious.

works.title: The Reckless Sleeper
works.hook: Magritte's dream objects: everyday things placed where they don't belong.
works.note: Painted with precise, almost illustrative realism, a bird, a mirror, a lit candle and an apple sit sunk into a slab beneath a sleeping man.

works.title: Celebes
works.hook: Ernst built this elephant-like machine from a photo of a corn bin.
works.note: Painted in Cologne, it pairs a hulking machine-beast with a headless nude wearing a surgical glove, realistic painting used to create a hallucinatory dream.
works.why: A hulking elephant-like machine beside a headless nude: the strange, dreamlike pairings at Surrealism's heart.

works.title: Black on Maroon
works.medium: Oil paint, acrylic paint, glue tempera and pigment on canvas
works.hook: One of the Seagram murals Rothko gave to Tate. They arrived on the day he died in 1970.
works.note: Rothko painted these brooding maroons and blacks for the Four Seasons restaurant in New York's Seagram Building, inspired by Michelangelo's staircase room in Florence, then withdrew.
works.why: Dark, window-like rectangles in an enveloping maroon field on a huge scale: colour carrying tragic emotion.

works.title: Summertime: Number 9A
works.medium: Oil paint, enamel paint and commercial paint on canvas
works.hook: Pollock dripped and poured paint onto canvas laid on the floor.
works.note: Oil, enamel and commercial house paint flung across a long horizontal canvas, its rhythm likened by critics to a line of dancing figures.
works.why: Skeins of dripped and flung paint across a long, low canvas: the energetic gesture of New York painting.

works.title: Marilyn Diptych
works.hook: Made in the weeks after Marilyn Monroe's death in 1962. Colour on the left, fading black and white on the right.
works.note: Warhol silkscreened fifty copies of a single publicity still from the film Niagara, turning a real woman into a repeated, mass-produced image.
works.why: One publicity photo of Marilyn silkscreened again and again, half in garish colour: celebrity as mass-produced Pop imagery.

works.title: Whaam!
works.medium: Acrylic paint and oil paint on canvas
works.hook: Based on a panel from a 1962 war comic. Note the Ben-Day dots.
works.note: Lichtenstein based it mainly on one comic panel by Irv Novick, enlarged into a four-metre two-panel canvas separating the firing plane from the explosion.
works.why: Ben-Day dots, bold black outlines and a 'WHAAM!' sound effect: a comic-book panel blown up into painting.

works.title: A Bigger Splash
works.hook: Two weeks to paint a splash that lasts two seconds, as Hockney put it.
works.note: Based on a photo in a book of swimming pools, rolled flat with acrylic and framed by an unpainted border like a Polaroid.
works.why: Flat, bright colour and crisp, clean shapes of a Californian pool: Pop's cool, advert-like look at modern life.

works.title: Mr and Mrs Clark and Percy
works.hook: Fashion designer Ossie Clark and textile designer Celia Birtwell. The cat is really Blanche; Percy was another of their cats.
works.note: Painted in flat acrylic, the couple appear near life-size in their Notting Hill bedroom: recognisable real people in a modern home, not abstract shapes.
works.why: Fashion-world celebrities posed in a crisp modern interior in flat acrylic colour: Pop's fascination with contemporary glamour.

works.title: The Resurrection, Cookham
works.hook: The dead rise in Spencer's home village of Cookham, Berkshire.
works.note: In Holy Trinity churchyard, Spencer's friends and family climb from their graves and over a stile, and his wife Hilda appears several times.
works.why: Villagers climb from graves in an English churchyard, solidly and simply drawn: modern painting rooted in a real British place.

works.title: Totes Meer (Dead Sea)
works.hook: 'Dead Sea': a graveyard of wrecked German aircraft, painted in WWII.
works.note: Based on Nash's sketches and photographs of a salvage dump at Cowley, near Oxford, where the wreckage looked to him like a surging sea under the moon.
works.why: Wrecked German planes piled like waves under a moon: a British painter's haunting view of the Second World War.

works.title: Ennui
works.note: Sickert paints a stale, airless room: an old man smoking at a table and a woman turned away, two people bored together among crowding objects.
works.why: A drab interior with a bored couple, painted in murky, broken colour: everyday modern British life, unglamorised.

works.title: Self-Portrait
works.note: Trained at the Slade and under Whistler, she paints herself in closely related, subdued tones and transparent glazes, quiet where others reached for bold colour or gold.
works.hook: She painted herself calm and watchful, in quiet browns.

works.title: Pelagos
works.medium: Elm and strings on oak base
works.hook: Hepworth carved it in St Ives; the strings echo the sea and sky of Cornwall.
works.note: A carved sculpture, not a painting: a nut-like elm form whose hollow is painted a cool light blue and crossed by taut strings.
works.why: Carved elm curling round a pale blue hollow strung with taut strings: modern British sculpture inspired by the Cornish sea.

works.title: Recumbent Figure
works.note: Carved from Green Hornton stone for an architect's Sussex garden, this reclining woman gazes out across the Downs, her body pierced by holes you can see through.
works.why: A reclining woman pierced by holes you can see through: modern British sculpture reshaping the human figure.

works.title: Girl with a White Dog
works.hook: Freud's first wife, Kitty Garman, painted with intense detail.
works.note: Freud painted his wife Kitty in tight, precise brushwork, a transitional work between his fine early style and the looser, thicker manner to come.
works.why: Every hair and fold rendered in tight, precise brushwork: the intense close looking of postwar British figurative painting.

works.title: Three Studies for Figures at the Base of a Crucifixion
works.hook: Shown in London in April 1945. It caused a sensation.
works.note: Three writhing creatures based on the Furies of Greek tragedy, in oil and pastel on cheap fibreboard against a harsh burnt orange.
works.why: Three distorted, half-human creatures against harsh orange: raw figurative painting from Britain near the end of the war.

works.title: Fall
works.hook: Op Art: one black line, repeated, that seems to move.
works.note: Riley hand-drew one curve, made a template from it, then painted black household paint over white so the waves tighten towards the bottom and seem to throb.
works.why: Black wavy lines tighten towards the bottom until the surface seems to throb: the optical dazzle of 1960s British painting.

works.title: Coming Out of School
works.note: Lowry's small 'matchstick' figures, casting no shadows, spill out of school into the industrial streets of North West England.
works.why: Tiny stick-like figures spill out of school into a grey town street: Lowry's own vision of the industrial North.

works.title: The Dance
works.medium: Acrylic paint on paper on canvas
works.note: Eight figures dance on a moonlit beach, including Rego herself with her husband Victor Willing, who died while she was painting it.
works.why: Solid, sculptural figures dance on a moonlit beach: figurative storytelling from a leading modern British painter.

works.title: Pharmacy
works.medium: Glass, faced particleboard, painted MDF, beech, ramin, wooden dowels, aluminium, pharmaceutical packaging, desks, office
works.hook: Hirst also opened a real restaurant called Pharmacy in Notting Hill.
works.note: Shelves of empty drug packaging, honey bowls and a buzzing insect-o-cutor turn a whole room into a chemist's, questioning the faith we place in medicine.
works.why: A whole room fitted out as a chemist's, with empty medicine packaging on shelves: YBA wit with everyday materials.

works.title: Studland Beach
works.hook: Painted on a Dorset beach. Bell simplifies figures into flat blocks of colour.
works.note: Bell borrowed the bright colours and bold forms of the Post-Impressionists shown in Roger Fry's exhibitions, and soon co-founded the Omega Workshops with him.
works.why: Figures seen only from behind, built from broad planes of colour facing the sea: bold, simplified Bloomsbury design.

works.title: Bathing
works.hook: Made for a Borough Polytechnic decoration scheme in 1911.
works.note: Male swimmers at the Serpentine in Hyde Park, then a men-only bathing spot, are stretched into athletic, almost scandalously suggestive poses.
works.why: Stylised swimmers stretched into a rhythmic pattern of bold colour: Bloomsbury decoration inspired by Post-Impressionism.

works.title: The Bar on East 13th
works.hook: Toor's take on Manet's A Bar at the Folies-Bergère, which belongs to the Courtauld, where his show is on.
works.note: Toor paints from memory and imagination, placing young queer South Asian men in a New York bar bathed in his characteristic emotional green.
works.why: An absinthe-green bar with an androgynous barmaid restaging Manet: contemporary painting rewriting art history around queer lives.

works.title: Bar Boy
works.place: Whitney Museum of American Art, New York
works.hook: One of the 2019 paintings Toor calls his 'coming out pictures'.
works.note: Toor's intimate scenes of young, brown, queer men in New York, washed in his signature green, borrow from Old Masters such as Watteau and Van Dyck.
works.why: A young man lit by his phone's glow in a green-washed bar: painting about life right now.

works.title: Three Friends in a Cab
works.hook: You sit in the back seat with three friends on a night out.
works.note: Toor paints recognisable people in intimate scenes, exploring queer and immigrant lives lived between cultures: storytelling, not pure shape and colour.

works.title: Ghost Ball
works.hook: A huge canvas, over three metres wide, now in the Pinault Collection. In his later work the figures turn looser and more ghostly.
works.note: Dancers swirl against a poisonous green, each absorbed in their own moment yet moving as one, a scene inspired by an Indian miniature painting.
works.why: Swirling dancers against a toxic, nocturnal green: figurative painting reworking art-historical references with a contemporary queer tone.

works.title: The Madonna with Canon van der Paele
works.hook: Painted in Bruges for Joris van der Paele, a canon of the city's church of St Donatian.
works.note: Van Eyck renders the ailing canon's stubble and veins, the weave of an oriental carpet and even his own reflection in St George's shield in meticulous oil.
works.why: The canon's stubble and veins, a carpet's weave, a reflection in a shield: Netherlandish oil detail at its finest.

works.title: The Academicians of the Royal Academy
works.hook: Reynolds, the Academy's first President, stands left of centre holding his ear trumpet.
works.note: Set in the life room at Old Somerset House with nude male models; the two women Academicians appear only as portraits hung on the wall.
works.why: Gentlemen artists chatting round a nude male model in the life room: a Georgian conversation piece packed with portraits.

works.title: George III in Coronation Robes
works.hook: George III founded the Royal Academy by personal act on 10 December 1768.
works.note: Painted from the very robes worn at the coronation, it became the official royal image, with copies sent to ambassadors and colonial governors.
works.why: The young king full-length in ermine-lined coronation robes, elegant and stately: the grand manner of official British portraiture.

works.title: Isabella
works.hook: The letters PRB are carved on Isabella's bench, a secret sign of the new Brotherhood.
works.note: Taken from Keats's poem, it almost eliminates shadow and intensifies clashing colours, while one brother violently kicks a frightened greyhound.
works.why: Bright, clashing colours with almost no shadow and a medieval banquet from Keats: the Brotherhood's crisp, literary style.

works.title: Claude Monet Painting by the Edge of a Wood
works.hook: Sargent caught his friend Monet at work outdoors, canvas propped on an easel in the open air.

works.title: Self-Portrait
works.hook: Fry was a painter as well as a critic; he coined 'Post-Impressionism' for his 1910 show.

works.title: Three Beauties of the Present Day
works.hook: The sitters were celebrities of Edo: a geisha and two teahouse waitresses.
works.note: A full-colour woodblock print with a background dusted with glittering mica; each woman wears a family crest that identifies her.
works.why: Three women's faces in fine black outlines on a glittering mica ground: an Edo woodblock print of beauties.

works.title: Secession Building, Vienna
works.hook: Joseph Maria Olbrich built it in 1897–98 as the group's own exhibition hall.

works.title: Self-Portrait with Physalis
works.hook: Schiele died in the 1918 flu pandemic, aged 28, only months after Klimt.
works.note: Sharp lines and bright red lantern fruits against dark tones make Schiele look fragile yet confident, painted as a pair with his portrait of Wally Neuzil.
works.why: Taut, wiry contours, a twisted pose and a sidelong stare: the raw psychological intensity of Vienna 1900.

works.title: Potsdamer Platz
works.hook: Kirchner's Berlin street scenes turned the city's nightlife sharp-edged and anxious.
works.note: Two prostitutes, one disguised in a war widow's black veil, stand on a steep traffic island under the station clock at midnight, in unreal pinks and glowing greens.
works.why: Elongated figures in flamingo red on a tilting green street: Expressionist distortion conveying the tension of the city.

works.title: Self-Portrait as a Soldier
works.place: Allen Memorial Art Museum, Oberlin, Ohio
works.hook: Kirchner painted himself with a severed hand, though he never lost one: an image of his fear that war would end his art.
works.note: Dark, cold colours, a sallow, angular face and a glassy-eyed nude model behind him: raw anxiety rather than Viennese ornament or Cubist analysis.
works.why: A mask-like face and a bloody stump where his painting hand should be: inner anguish through distortion and harsh colour.

works.title: Street, Dresden
works.place: Museum of Modern Art, New York
works.hook: Kirchner co-founded Die Brücke in Dresden in 1905; he reworked this picture in 1919.
works.note: Mask-like faces with vacant eyes crowd Dresden's fashionable Königstrasse in heightened colours, capturing how Kirchner felt 'carried along' by the city crowd.
works.why: Mask-like faces crowd a shrill pink pavement: Expressionist distortion and clashing colour conveying inner unease.

works.title: Blue Horse I
works.hook: For Marc, blue stood for the spiritual.
works.note: A young blue foal tilts its head towards us in a landscape of clashing complementary colours such as vermilion and light green, colour chosen for feeling, not nature.
works.why: A blue horse before hills of carmine, yellow and violet: colour chosen for feeling and spirit, not nature.

works.title: Breakfast
works.place: Museum of Modern Art, New York
works.hook: Gris pasted printed papers into this still life, the papier collé technique Braque introduced in 1912.
works.note: Real wallpaper stands in for the wall, and a newspaper clipping reading 'GRIS' doubles as his signature among cups and a coffeepot seen from several angles.
works.why: Pasted wallpaper and newsprint, and a coffeepot seen from several angles at once: Cubist collage and faceting.

works.title: Poster for the Cabaret Voltaire
works.hook: Słodki designed the poster for the opening of the Cabaret Voltaire in Zurich in 1916.

works.title: Saatchi Gallery, Chelsea, London
works.hook: Charles Saatchi's gallery has been in the Duke of York's HQ off the King's Road since 2008.

works.title: Plaques at 46 Gordon Square, Bloomsbury
works.hook: Vanessa Bell and her siblings moved here in 1904; Keynes later lived here too.

works.title: Roger Fry plaque, 33 Fitzroy Square, London
works.hook: The Omega Workshops ran from this house from 1913 to 1919.

works.title: Plaque to Sir Henry Tate, sugar magnate and founder of the Tate Gallery
works.hook: Tate's sugar fortune paid for the gallery at Millbank, opened in 1897.

works.title: John Julius Angerstein (replica of an 1816 portrait)
works.place: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
works.hook: Parliament bought 38 of Angerstein's paintings in 1824 to found the National Gallery.

works.title: A Private View at the Royal Academy, 1881
works.hook: Frith packed the RA's annual exhibition with celebrities, including Oscar Wilde and Gladstone.

works.title: Sotheby's, New Bond Street, London
works.hook: Sotheby's has held its London sales on New Bond Street since 1917.

works.artist: Thomas Rowlandson and Augustus Charles Pugin
works.title: Auction Room, Christie's (from The Microcosm of London)
works.hook: A sale in progress at Christie's Pall Mall rooms, drawn for Ackermann's Microcosm of London.

works.title: Messe Basel, Hall 2
works.hook: Art Basel fills the Messe Basel halls every June.

works.title: Regent's Park, London
works.hook: Frieze London and Frieze Masters put up their tents here every October.

works.title: Somerset House, London
works.hook: The Courtauld Gallery occupies the Strand wing of Somerset House.

works.title: Officer and Laughing Girl
works.hook: Toor's Museum Boys hung in the same room as this Vermeer at Frick Madison in 2021.

works.title: Central Pavilion, Giardini della Biennale, Venice
works.hook: The Biennale's main exhibition is split between this pavilion and the Arsenale.

works.title: Mangroves in the Sundarbans
works.hook: The Sundarbans, shared by India and Bangladesh, is the world's largest mangrove forest.

works.title: Self-Portrait with Bandaged Ear
works.hook: Painted in Arles in January 1889, about a week after he left hospital. Behind him hangs a Japanese print.
works.note: Thick impasto strokes give energy to a raw image: van Gogh in a blue fur cap and green coat, a canvas waiting on the easel beside him.
works.why: Thick, directional strokes of bold colour build a raw self-image: Post-Impressionist paint carrying personal feeling.

works.title: The Bedroom
works.hook: His own room in the Yellow House in Arles. He later painted two more versions.
works.note: Van Gogh painted his room in 'flat, plain tints like Japanese prints', removing shadows so that looking at it would 'rest the mind'.
works.why: Flat, plain tints and no shadows, like Japanese prints: colour and form simplified to express a feeling of rest.

works.title: The Yellow House
works.hook: The house on Place Lamartine in Arles where he rented rooms in 1888.
works.note: Van Gogh wanted 'a sulphur sun' and 'a pure cobalt sky', and included the restaurant where he dined every day and a passing train.
works.why: A sulphur-yellow house under an intense cobalt-blue sky: bold colour pushed beyond nature, a Post-Impressionist trait.

works.title: Almond Blossom
works.hook: A gift for Theo and Jo when their son, named Vincent after him, was born.
works.note: Flowering branches, for van Gogh a symbol of awakening and hope, are flattened into bold pattern, reflecting his love of Japanese woodcuts.
works.why: Blossoming branches against a flat blue sky, outlined like a Japanese print: simplified Post-Impressionist form and colour.

works.title: A Wheatfield, with Cypresses
works.hook: Painted at Saint-Rémy in September 1889, a studio version of a view he first painted outdoors that summer.
works.note: Signature swirling brushstrokes animate the wheat, cypresses, clouds and even the blue Alpilles, binding the whole landscape together in restless movement.
works.why: Thick, swirling strokes run through wheat, cypress and clouds alike: one painter's restless, personal touch binding everything.

works.title: St Ives
works.medium: Oil paint, graphite and crayon on cardboard
works.hook: Given to Tate by Ben Nicholson in 1966.
works.note: Wallis was self-taught, never had an art lesson, and took up painting around 70 after his wife's death, painting from memory.

works.title: The Blue Ship
works.medium: Oil paint on board on wood
works.hook: Painted from memory, like all his ships.
works.note: Self-taught Wallis ignored perspective, sized things by importance and painted with ship's paint on scraps of packing-box cardboard, so his scenes resemble early maps.
works.why: A ship and sea drawn without perspective, things sized by importance: the naive directness modern British artists admired.

works.title: Schooner under the Moon
works.medium: Oil paint and graphite on cardboard on plywood
works.hook: A schooner, the kind of sailing ship he crewed as a young man.
works.note: Self-taught, Wallis began painting at around seventy, using ship's paint on scraps of cardboard and sizing things by importance rather than perspective.
works.why: A ship and moon on scrap card, sized by importance rather than perspective: the naive vision British modernists championed.

works.title: Houses at St Ives, Cornwall
works.hook: His own town, painted on cardboard without perspective.
works.note: Wallis used ship paint and sized things by importance rather than distance, so his town reads almost like an early map.

works.title: Voyage to Labrador
works.hook: A memory of his Atlantic crossings as a young sailor.
works.note: Wallis began painting around seventy after his wife died, using a limited palette and simple flat shapes, a naive directness championed by Ben Nicholson and Christopher Wood.
works.why: Boats and sea reduced to flat, simple shapes in a few colours: self-taught directness prized by modern British painters.

works.title: The Pool of London
works.hook: Sent to London to paint the Thames, Derain turned it into blazing colour.
works.note: Commissioned by the dealer Ambroise Vollard, these Thames views burst with riotous colour, radically unlike earlier views of the city by Whistler or Monet.
works.why: Boats, water and sky in bold, clashing colours laid on freely: colour used for its own sake, not copying nature.

works.title: Untitled (Stairs)
works.hook: Whiteread casts the empty spaces of everyday things, here a staircase.

works.title: Untitled (Studio)
works.place: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
works.hook: Inspired by his childhood visit to the studio of his hero, painter Charles White.
works.why: A busy Black artist's workshop full of art-making: the old 'artist's studio' theme recast with Black figures.

works.title: Mogamma (A Painting in Four Parts): Part 3
works.hook: Over four and a half metres tall. Its three sister paintings live in Abu Dhabi, Atlanta and Houston.
works.why: Building outlines buried under clouds of marks: no picture of Cairo, just its energy. Pure abstraction.

works.title: Mogamma (A Painting in Four Parts): Part 2
works.hook: She researched public squares in cities around the world for the four Mogamma paintings.
works.why: Layer on layer of fine lines and smudges with no single subject: Abstract art built from real architecture.

works.title: Stadia II
works.hook: Begun as the US drummed up support for the Iraq War, the series asks why crowds love a spectacle.
works.why: A stadium outline dissolves among flags and marks: abstraction charged with world events.

works.title: Black City
works.hook: The see-through structures include wartime bunkers, such as Hitler's Atlantic Wall in Normandy.
works.why: Aggressive swarms of black marks attack ghostly architecture: abstraction as a battlefield of energy.

works.title: Retopistics: A Renegade Excavation
works.place: Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art, Bentonville
works.hook: Its shapes are traced from airport plans, maps and subway platforms. Over five metres wide.
works.why: Fragments of plans and maps with no single viewpoint: abstraction built from the shapes of cities.

works.title: 10pm Saturday
works.hook: Like all her figures, this person is invented, not a real sitter.
works.why: An imagined Black figure in loose, quick strokes: Black figuration in the grand portrait tradition.

works.title: The Black Watchful
works.place: Art Gallery of South Australia, Adelaide
works.hook: Two metres tall and, like most of her canvases, painted in a single day.
works.why: A two-metre canvas of an invented Black figure: Old Master scale given to a Black subject.

works.title: Razorbill
works.hook: Her poetic titles, like this seabird's name, are clues rather than explanations.
works.why: An imagined figure with no clues to era or place: the timeless Black portrait she is known for.

works.title: The Generosity
works.hook: She paints from scrapbooks, memory and imagination, never from a model in the room.
works.why: An invented Black sitter in oils, outside any real time: everyday Black life given the weight of grand painting.

works.title: No Woman, No Cry
works.hook: Glow-in-the-dark paint hides the words 'R.I.P. Stephen Lawrence', visible only when the lights go down.
works.why: Resin, glitter, map pins and elephant dung on one canvas: the YBA appetite for daring materials.

works.title: Double Captain Shit and the Legend of the Black Stars
works.hook: Captain Shit is Ofili's own Black superhero, a playful send-up of 1970s comic heroes like Luke Cage.
works.why: A cheeky comic-book hero in glitter and dung: YBA wit poking at pop culture and stereotypes.

works.title: Blue Devils
works.hook: Inspired by the blue devil characters of Trinidad's Carnival; he has lived on the island since 2005.
works.why: Oil and charcoal instead of glitter and dung: the YBA showman's later, quieter painting from Trinidad.

works.title: The Upper Room
works.hook: Thirteen spotlit monkey paintings in a walnut room designed by architect David Adjaye.
works.why: A whole room as artwork, with paintings resting on dung: the YBA taste for theatrical, immersive installations.

works.title: Between the Two my Heart is Balanced
works.hook: A reply to a James Tissot picture of a soldier in a boat between two women.
works.why: Two Black women take over a Victorian scene and tear up colonial charts: Black Arts Movement history-rewriting.

works.title: Ankledeep
works.hook: Shredded paper falls from one woman's hand. Some see a map of the past being torn up.
works.why: Two Black women at the centre, tearing up the past: the British Black Arts Movement's new heroines.

works.title: Man in A Shirt Drawer
works.hook: Painted inside an old wooden drawer, brass handles and all.
works.why: A Black man's portrait painted on found furniture: the movement's urge to recover people history forgot.

works.title: The Carrot Piece
works.hook: A white man dangles a carrot. The Black woman ignores him and walks off.
works.why: Painted cut-out figures with a sharp political joke about the art world: classic 1980s Black Arts Movement satire.

works.title: Freedom and Change
works.hook: Her earliest work about women together, made of wood, textiles and cardboard.
works.why: Painted cut-outs in wood, textiles and cardboard: the movement's bold, homemade, theatrical style of the early 1980s.

works.title: Ink Splash II
works.hook: Up close it is flattened bottle tops and copper wire; from across the room it looks like spilled ink on cloth.
works.why: A metal 'cloth' hung loosely in folds: it changes shape each time it is installed.

works.title: Dusasa II
works.place: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
works.hook: The title means a patchwork made together by townspeople, like his team of assistants.
works.why: Thousands of bottle tops wired into one sheet over seven metres wide: a hanging that reshapes the wall and room around it.

works.title: Between Earth and Heaven
works.place: Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
works.hook: Gold, red and black metal imitates fine woven silk, inspired by Ghanaian kente cloth.
works.why: Thousands of crushed metal pieces ripple like fabric: found materials remade on a huge scale.

works.title: Another Place
works.hook: The copper wire stays bendy, so the work takes a new form at every showing.
works.why: Bottle caps joined with pliable copper wire: a metal 'cloth' that takes a new shape each time it is hung.

works.title: Solemn Crowd at Dawn
works.hook: Before bottle tops, he carved and painted wood: this crowd dates from 1989.
works.why: Carved and painted wood standing in for a crowd: the wood-based work he made before his metal hangings.

works.title: Infinity Mirrored Room – Filled with the Brilliance of Life
works.hook: Made for her 2012 Tate retrospective: pulsing lights repeat in mirrors and a shallow pool.
works.why: Tiny lights multiplied by mirrors and water in a room you walk into: the endless space at the heart of installation art.

works.title: Chandelier of Grief
works.hook: A spinning chandelier repeats forever; the title pairs beauty with sadness.
works.why: One spinning chandelier repeated by mirrored walls: Kusama's infinity, with you caught inside it.

works.title: The Passing Winter
works.hook: Peer through round holes in this mirrored cube to see reflections without end.
works.why: Mirrored glass inside a small box: the endless, repeating space behind her Infinity Mirror Rooms.

works.title: Tree
works.hook: Dead branches from southern China's mountains, joined into one tree with big industrial bolts.
works.why: Natural from afar, clearly assembled up close: everyday material rebuilt as a statement.

works.title: Table and Pillar
works.hook: A Qing dynasty pillar rises 4.6 metres straight through a Qing dynasty table.
works.why: A Qing pillar driven straight through a Qing table: Ai cuts up real antiques to question tradition and value.

works.title: Sunflower Seeds
works.hook: Tate owns about 8 million of the 100 million porcelain seeds, each sculpted and painted by hand in Jingdezhen.
works.why: Countless tiny handmade seeds spread across a floor: installation art that turns mass labour into one vast landscape.

works.title: Shibboleth
works.hook: The 167-metre crack was filled in afterwards, but a line still marks the floor.
works.why: The gallery floor itself becomes the artwork: a crack running the length of the hall.

works.title: Untitled
works.hook: Household furniture filled with cement becomes a silent monument to people who vanished.
works.why: Ordinary wooden furniture made useless with cement: everyday objects carrying grief.

works.title: Untitled
works.hook: She first stacked plaster-stiffened shirts around 1990 to mourn murdered plantation workers.
works.why: Piles of white shirts pierced by steel bars: the body suggested but never shown.

works.title: Atrabiliarios
works.hook: Worn shoes, mostly of disappeared women, sealed into the wall behind cow bladder stitched with surgical thread.
works.why: Niches cut into the gallery wall hold personal objects: the room becomes a memorial.

works.title: The Weather Project
works.hook: A half-circle of lamps doubled by a mirrored ceiling looked like a full sun.
works.why: A whole hall filled with mist, light and mirrors: visitors became part of the work.

works.title: Stardust particle
works.hook: A motor turns this steel and glass ball while a spotlight scatters light around the room.
works.why: Light, reflection and movement are the real materials, filling the space around the object.

works.title: Your Double-Lighthouse Projection
works.hook: Built from fluorescent tubes, plywood and a mylar screen: he sculpts with light itself.
works.why: A structure you step inside, bathed in coloured light that changes how you see.

works.title: Fons Americanus
works.hook: Her 13-metre 2019 Turbine Hall fountain reworked London's Victoria Memorial to tell of slavery.
works.why: A full-size public fountain built indoors: a monument you walk around and question.

works.title: Keys to the Coop
works.hook: A linocut: a black silhouette of a girl chasing a chicken, cut out of the white page.
works.why: A genteel silhouette style turned to a disturbing scene: polite craft, brutal story.

works.title: Grub for Sharks: A Concession to the Negro Populace
works.hook: Made of cut paper, the old craft of portrait silhouettes she turned to darker stories.
works.why: Black cut-paper figures spread wide across a white wall, like a panorama to walk along.

works.title: Me carry my head on my home on my head
works.place: Whitney Museum of American Art, New York
works.hook: Over two metres tall, built from paint, ink, sequins and cut-out pictures on plastic.
works.why: A hybrid figure of roots and flesh: a future body pieced together from many worlds, typical of Afrofuturism.

works.title: The Seated III
works.place: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
works.hook: One of four bronzes that filled the Met's empty facade niches, which had waited since 1902.
works.why: Part celestial being, part African queen: an Afrofuturist update of the ancient caryatid.

works.title: You were always on my mind
works.hook: Plastic pearls and glittering particles sit alongside ink and paint on clear plastic film.
works.why: Glossy magazine scraps and pearls fuse into one strange body: Afrofuturist collage imagining new kinds of being.

works.title: Chorus Line
works.hook: Eight collages of distorted, full-bodied women hang together like a chorus line of dancers.
works.why: Watercolour and collage figures repeat in a row, each one a patched-together hybrid from another world.

works.title: Untitled Film Still #21
works.place: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
works.hook: She plays a Hitchcock-style career girl alone on a city street. The film never existed.
works.why: A fake movie still copying Hollywood's look: Pictures Generation art borrowing the language of mass media.

works.title: Untitled Film Still #48
works.hook: Shot in 1979, this print was made from the negative in 1998.
works.why: Grainy black and white and a lonely figure: a film noir moment staged for the camera, Pictures Generation style.

works.title: Untitled
works.place: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
works.hook: Here Sherman becomes Marilyn Monroe, or rather Norma Jean, out of her famous sex-kitten role.
works.why: A star's familiar image restaged by the artist herself: the Pictures Generation questioning celebrity pictures.

works.title: Untitled #97
works.hook: From the early 1980s, when Sherman swapped black and white for colour.
works.why: Bright colour and a tense, staged pose: Sherman acting out an invented role, Pictures Generation style.

works.title: Rhythm 0
works.hook: For six hours in Naples, visitors could use any of 72 objects on her, including a loaded gun.
works.why: Only photos remain of a live action: performance art, where the artist's body is the material.

works.title: Rhythm 5
works.hook: She lay inside a burning star, passed out as the fire ate the oxygen, and was pulled out.
works.why: Black and white photos record a risky live event: performance art testing the limits of the body.

works.title: Rhythm 10
works.hook: She stabbed between her spread fingers with a row of knives, then tried to repeat her own cuts.
works.why: A sequence of photos documents a ritual done with her own hand: endurance as performance art.

works.title: Cleaning the Mirror
works.hook: Five stacked screens show her scrubbing a grimy skeleton, bone by bone.
works.why: Stacked monitors replay a long, repetitive action: performance art made for the camera.

works.title: The Hero
works.place: National Museum of Women in the Arts, Washington, DC
works.hook: Made just after her father, a wartime partisan hero, died. She sits still on a white horse.
works.why: The artist herself, motionless with a white flag: stillness and presence, the heart of her performance art.

works.title: Casspirs Full of Love
works.place: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
works.hook: The title plays on Casspirs, armoured police vehicles used to patrol Black townships under apartheid.
works.why: Heads stacked in boxes, scratched in drypoint: the same urgent hand drawing that powers his animated films.

works.title: Untitled (Woman Turning into a Telephone)
works.hook: A linocut caught mid-change, like one frame from one of his transforming animations.
works.why: One shape morphing into another: the logic of his animated films, frozen into a single print.

works.title: Felix in Exile
works.hook: Made by drawing in charcoal, filming, rubbing out and redrawing, frame after frame.
